title: Casing The HPC And AI-Sci Market With Hyperion Research
gist: According to Hyperion Research's SC26 data, on-premises HPC and AI-for-Science system spending rose 19.9% to $16.48B in 1H 2026 on just 4.4% unit growth, and Dell (+67.7% to $3.93B) overtook HPE ($3.44B, +1.1%) as revenue leader. Timothy Prickett Morgan estimates HPC holds only 3–4% of the 31–37M GPU/XPU fleet worldwide. Hyperion forecasts combined on-prem and cloud HPC/AI-Sci infrastructure spending of $135B by 2030.

insights.claim: According to Hyperion Research, worldwide spending on on-premises HPC and AI-for-Science systems rose 19.9 percent to $16.48 billion in the first half of 2026, while unit shipments grew only 4.4 percent versus the first half of 2025.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Revenue is growing far faster than units, so HPC system vendors are getting growth from bigger systems and higher prices more than from volume.
insights.locator: The revenues in the chart above

insights.claim: The gap between 19.9 percent revenue growth and 4.4 percent unit growth in on-premises HPC and AI-Sci systems in 1H 2026 comes from more nodes per system, slightly more CPUs per system, and price increases for CPUs, GPUs, DRAM, and flash.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Component inflation in memory and accelerators is being passed through into HPC system revenue.

insights.claim: Timothy Prickett Morgan suspects HPC centers are being conservative and staying one or two generations behind on CPUs and GPUs to lower capital outlay. Evidence is that many Grace-Hopper and Intel Xeon-Hopper systems are still entering the Top500 even though Grace-Blackwell has been available for two years.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Prior-generation accelerators keep a longer tail of demand in HPC, which supports older Hopper-class products and lowers ASPs for this segment.
insights.quote: More current GPUs are too scarce and too expensive for most HPC centers.

insights.claim: In the first half of 2026, Dell became the revenue leader in on-premises HPC and AI-Sci systems. Its sales grew 67.7 percent to $3.93 billion, while Hewlett Packard Enterprise grew only 1.1 percent to $3.44 billion. HPE had led the market for years after acquiring SGI and Cray.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: This is a share shift toward Dell in technical computing; watch whether it holds in second-half data released at ISC27.

insights.claim: Dell's HPC share gain may come from GPU allocations by Nvidia or AMD. Dell has had preferential treatment from Nvidia for AI systems over the past two years, which the author attributes to the relationship between Michael Dell and Jensen Huang. The article notes that Huang no longer runs Nvidia.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Access to GPU supply may now decide OEM share in HPC, so vendor relationships with Nvidia matter as much as the product.
insights.quote: It was a billionaire thing between Michael Dell and Jensen Huang
insights.locator: It is hard to say if this

insights.claim: HPE may still lead Dell in aggregate FP64 flops sold in HPC and AI-Sci. HPE might be selling more CPU-only machines for traditional modeling and simulation, while Dell sells more accelerator-equipped machines that are not used only for GenAI.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Revenue rank may not reflect capability share, so a mix shift toward GPU systems flatters Dell's dollar figures.
insights.locator: It could turn out that HPE

insights.claim: Below Dell and HPE, vendor revenue drops off quickly. Dozens of OEMs and ODMs together accounted for $9.12 billion in 1H 2026 HPC and AI-Sci system sales, up 13.8 percent versus 19.9 percent for the overall market, so Dell's size and growth are lifting the market average.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Without Dell, the HPC market grew more slowly than the headline figure, which concentrates the growth story on one vendor.
insights.quote: Dell’s growth and its size are lifting the class average bigtime.
insights.locator: The revenues per vendor drop off

themes.theme: HPC is a sliver of the AI fleet

insights.claim: Extrapolating Hyperion Research's 2017–2025 installed-base trend, Timothy Prickett Morgan expects about 1.2 million GPU accelerators to be installed in HPC and AI-Sci systems worldwide by the end of 2026.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: This gives a baseline size for HPC GPU demand when sizing accelerator markets.
insights.locator: To my eyes, we keep going

insights.claim: By the author's rough estimate, the global installed base is 18–20 million GPUs plus 13–17 million custom AI XPUs. These include Google TPUs (9–11 million), Amazon Trainium (about 3 million) and Inferentia (1–2 million), plus hundreds of thousands each of Microsoft Maia and Meta MTIA. Chinese custom XPUs are negligible.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Custom silicon already makes up a large share of the AI accelerator fleet, and Google TPUs lead it. This matters for Nvidia share and for custom-ASIC suppliers.
insights.quote: The Chinese custom XPUs are noise in this data, and China hates that this is true.
insights.locator: Doing some back of the envelope math

insights.claim: HPC and AI-Sci systems hold only about 3–4 percent of the roughly 31–37 million GPUs and XPUs running worldwide. HPC and AI-Sci spending is several tens of billions of dollars a year, while AI training and inference spending is two to three orders of magnitude larger.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: HPC is now a niche market for accelerators, so vendor roadmaps will be set by AI demand rather than by HPC needs such as FP64.
insights.quote: The AI tail that used to be on the HPC dog a decade and a half ago has been cloned

insights.claim: Hyperion Research forecasts that on-premises HPC and AI-Sci server sales will roughly triple in the decade ending 2030. That is steady growth, but not the exponential growth GenAI has seen. Divisional, departmental, and workgroup systems are expected to keep roughly the same share of sales as large supercomputers.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: The HPC server market offers steady, non-exponential growth, and its mix by system size is stable.

insights.claim: Earl Joseph of Hyperion Research says the broader HPC and AI-Sci market, including storage, middleware, applications, services, and cloud compute, networking, and storage, will exceed $100 billion in 2030, against $54 billion in on-premises system sales.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Spending on software, services, and cloud is about as large as spending on hardware, which widens the addressable market beyond system OEMs.
insights.locator: Joseph says that the broader HPC

insights.claim: Hyperion Research expects cloud spending on HPC and AI-Sci capacity to grow nearly 5x from 2022 to about $30 billion in 2030. North America will lead, ahead of EMEA and Asia/Pacific.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Cloud is the fastest-growing channel for HPC, which benefits hyperscalers that rent capacity for scientific workloads.

insights.claim: Hyperion Research puts combined on-premises and cloud infrastructure spending for HPC and AI-Sci workloads at just over $40 billion in 2022, rising about 3.4x to $135 billion in 2030.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: This is a top-down figure for the size of HPC infrastructure spending to 2030.

insights.claim: Annual cloud spending on HPC looks much smaller than on-premises spending, but on-premises purchases cover about five years of use. Comparing five years of cloud spending with one year of on-premises purchases brings the two close together, with on-premises probably only slightly larger. Many HPC centers do both and are expected to keep doing so.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Annual spending figures understate cloud's real share of HPC compute-hours, so a hybrid model is likely to persist rather than one side winning.
insights.quote: If you add up five years of cloud spending and compare it to the on premises spending for a particular year
insights.locator: It may look like cloud spending

insights.claim: Both on-premises HPC revenues and cloud rental revenues include price increases from higher component costs, and these are being passed on to end customers.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Part of the HPC growth in dollars is inflation rather than more compute, so adjust the forecasts before treating them as demand.
